newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Scott Thomas turns steamy in English Patient.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Scott Thomas turns steamy in English Patient.

text.p: Years of playing brittle upper class Englishwomen have come to a sudden and steamy end for Kristin Scott Thomas with her role as the passionate Katherine Clifton in the Oscar-nominated film "The English Patient".

She won worldwife fame in "Four Weddings and a Funeral" as Fiona, the woman who never stood a chance as Andie McDowell won Hugh Grant's favours, one of several films in which she was typecast to play frosty, thwarted women.
"I thought I was going to be funny in 'Four Weddings', but I turned out to be the tragic element," she says.

In "The English Patient", directed by Anthony Minghella and written by Booker Prize winner Michael Ondaatje, Scott Thomas is an emotional blonde hell-bent on a reckless adulterous affair which has tragic consequences. And she loved it.
"I felt the part of Katherine was written specially for me, so I wrote an impassioned letter to the director begging to play her," Scott Thomas said in a magazine interview.
As married Katherine she embarks on a destructive affair with Hungarian Count Laszlo de Almasy played by Ralph Fiennes of "Schindler's List" fame.
SCOTT THOMAS SAYS SHE HAS NO HOLLYWOOD AMBITIONS
Scott Thomas, 36, says she doesn't enjoy acting but can't do anything else. She has no intention of trying to make it big in Hollywood.
"I wouldn't know whose boots to lick and even if I did, I wouldn't know how to do it," she said.
Born in Dorset, England, Scott Thomas has lived in Paris for 18 years. For the last 15 years she has been married to French gynaecologist Francois Oliviennes.
"He is a great driving force behind my career and very supportive," said Scott Thomas.
The couple live with their two children Hannah, 7, and Joseph, 4, in an apartment on the Left Bank in Paris.

A product of a convent school and the exclusive Cheltenham Ladies' College, Scott Thomas enrolled with the Central School of Speech and Drama in London at 18. This project was abandoned when she says she was told she couldn't act.

"It (Cheltenham Ladies' College) destroyed every ounce of self-confidence I ever hoped to have. It turned me into somebody who though the world stopped at the middle classes, somebody who thought brains were bad news," she said.
After working as a waitress, receptionist and a secretary, Scott Thomas moved to Paris as an au-pair.
In Paris friends persuaded her to return to study drama at the Ecole Nationale de Theatre where she met her husband.
FILM CAREER BEGAN WITH A FLOP

Her first role was in the film "Under the Cherry Moon" with the pop star Prince. The film flopped, but Scott Thomas went on to win an Evening Standard award for most promising newcomer for her portrayal of the upper crust Lady Brenda in "A Handful of Dust", based on the novel by Evelyn Waugh.
She was then chosen by Roman Polanski to play Hugh Grant's frigid wife in "Bitter Moon". It was Grant who got her the role of the frosty Fiona in "Four Weddings and a Funeral" three years ago.
That same year she had a role in Philip Haas's Victorian sexual melodrama "Angels And Insects", an adaptation of an A S Byatt novella.
Last year she notched up another success as Lady Anne in Ian McKellen's controversial adaptation of "Richard III" and had a cameo role in the Hollywood blockbuster "Mission impossible".
Future roles include a part in the film of Alan Ayckbourn's "Revenger's Comedies" and a French farce "Amours et Confusions".
Scott Thomas is the eldest of five children. Her father, a pilot in the Royal Navy, was killed in a flying accident when she was five.
Six later her stepfather died in another flying accident.
"You can't believe it when you lose one father and then another six years later. Now I'd really like to have a father, particularly when I see Francois with our children," she said.
